text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Dental pain and infection safety today: ibuprofen 400 mg with acetaminophen 1 g, alternating, for up to a week, and no opioid; no antibiotic, because the swelling is localized, there is no fever above 38 °C, no trismus and no spread, and drainage is arranged within 24 hours; go to the emergency department at once for swelling spreading to the eye, the floor of the mouth or the neck, difficulty swallowing or breathing, trouble opening the mouth, or a fever
  • Urgent oral and maxillofacial surgery consultation within 24 hours for imaging, drainage of the abscess and extraction or other definitive treatment of the broken molar, with an assessment of her gums
  • Type 2 diabetes: metformin extended-release, started slowly; diabetes self-management education and medical nutrition therapy in the clinic's program; A1c every three months until at goal; eye screening, a comprehensive foot examination and kidney tests at diagnosis and yearly; blood pressure goal below 130/80; sick-day rules for metformin; endocrinology only if the A1c is not at goal by six months
  • Weight and health without stigma: person-first language, weight discussed only with her permission, goals she sets for strength and movement, and the medicines that lower both glucose and weight (GLP-1 receptor agonists) explained for her to consider
  • Knee osteoarthritis: a walking and strengthening program, diclofenac gel as needed, and a cane or knee support for long site visits if helpful; no imaging needed for a clinical diagnosis
  • Mood screening: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at intake and at the end of the episode
  • Periodontitis and the abscess: chlorhexidine rinse for two weeks after the extraction; scaling and root planing of all teeth by the dental team about six weeks after the extraction, then periodontal maintenance every three months; the two-way link with diabetes explained (periodontal treatment can lower A1c, and better glucose control helps the gums heal)
  • Semaglutide once weekly, 0.25 mg for four weeks, then 0.5 mg, with small meals and stopping eating when full to limit nausea; chosen with her for glucose and weight after the dental infection had settled; an SGLT2 inhibitor is not indicated without kidney or heart disease; muscle-strengthening exercise and enough protein to protect muscle and bone as weight falls
  • Cardiovascular risk: atorvastatin 20 mg daily (moderate intensity), as advised for adults 40 to 75 with diabetes; lipids and ALT at about eight to twelve weeks
  • Acute cystitis: nitrofurantoin for five days after a urine culture; fluids; metformin continued while she eats and drinks normally, and paused if she vomits or cannot keep fluids down; the semaglutide step up to 0.5 mg delayed one week; return at once for fever, flank pain, vomiting or symptoms not better in 48 hours
  • Cancer screening by age: screening mammography (every two years from 40), fecal immunochemical test yearly or colonoscopy (from 45), and primary HPV testing every five years (30 to 65); no search for bone cancer, because nothing in her history, examination or blood tests points to one; bone health through weight-bearing and strengthening exercise, calcium from food and adequate vitamin D, with bone density testing at 65 or sooner if a risk factor appears

resource.title: Hatshepsut synthetic care plan
resource.description: Care for a 48-year-old woman with a painful swollen jaw from a dental abscess, and type 2 diabetes found on screening, as current guidance advises and without weight stigma: recognize the warning signs of spreading odontogenic infection; give an NSAID with acetaminophen for dental pain and no opioid; withhold antibiotics when the abscess is localized, there is no systemic involvement and definitive treatment is available the next day (ADA 2019); arrange urgent drainage and extraction; diagnose diabetes from two abnormal results in one sample; start metformin, then add a GLP-1 receptor agonist chosen for weight and glucose (ADA Standards of Care 2026), with an SGLT2 inhibitor not indicated without kidney or heart disease; start a statin as the Standards advise for adults 40 to 75 with diabetes; screen for eye, foot and kidney complications; explain the two-way link between periodontitis and diabetes and arrange periodontal therapy; manage knee osteoarthritis with exercise and a topical NSAID; and keep up cancer screening by age (mammography, colorectal and cervical) and bone health, without a search for bone cancer when nothing in the modern episode points to one. The modern episode is a teaching case, not a claim about her real illnesses, which cannot be known from ancient remains whose identity is debated.
